name: Absolutism (European history)
summary: Absolutism holds that sovereign power should rest wholly in a monarch, unrestrained by legislatures, churches or social elites. It is justified by divine right and by the theory that sovereignty is indivisible and perpetual, though classic theorists still bind the ruler to natural and divine law. In practice it centralised law, built standing armies and bureaucracies, subordinated the church and favoured mercantilist economics.
scope: Classical European absolutism of roughly 1600 to 1789: monarchical power that is not subject to regularized challenge by church, legislature, nobility or courts, justified by divine right of kings and by indivisible sovereignty (Britannica, s5, s6, s8). Its defining sources name Louis XIV as the epitome, Bossuet and James I as its theorists and, with the dispute noted by the Stanford Encyclopedia, Bodin (s2). Britannica notes the same label is also used for modern dictators (s5) and for Hobbes's pragmatic case; this audit covers the early modern European doctrine only, and excludes enlightened absolutism and modern dictatorships.
